newsitem.title: USA: Funds for a flat market.
newsitem.headline: Funds for a flat market.

text.p: What if the stock market doesn't do anything?

Such a scenario is hard to imagine these days, after years of soaring stock prices punctuated by occasional corrections, most notably the 1987 stock market crash. Thus, most investors think in terms of big gains or big losses and they design their portfolios accordingly.

On the one hand, fund investors want to share in gains if the stock market soars. That hope leads them to buy shares in highly aggressive stock funds that invest in fast-growing companies. But the same investors also worry that they will suffer hideous losses if the stock market suddenly plummets.
As a result, some of them have shifted savings into money market funds or other cash holdings.
But buying the most aggressive funds or retreating to cash probably won't work if the stock market decides to do nothing for the next few years. And that is a real possibility.

Many market watchers point out that stocks have returned 15.3 percent annually during the past decade. That's considerably higher than the 10.7 percent annualized return for stocks during the past 71 years. Thus, they expect returns to revert to more normal or even subnormal levels.
As for a bear market, it's hard to imagine a sustained plunge in prices as long as inflation remains modest and baby boomers continue to save for retirement, fuelling demand for stocks.

What should fund investors do in a flat market? One solution is to add current income to the mix in their portfolio. That doesn't mean you should shift all of your money to bonds. But it might mean investing in funds that hold shares of companies paying above-average dividends.
The dividends from those stocks will provide current income that you can reinvest, which can be a tremendous advantage in a sluggish market.
For example, say that stocks only produce capital gains of 6 percent annually. If you hold shares of blue chips that pay 3 percent dividends, you'll generate a 9 percent annual return.

And what if stocks plummet, after all? In that case, your dividends will help cushion the fall. And your funds' stocks will probably hold up relatively well, since investors during bad times tend to bid up prices of stocks with high dividends.

One fund worth considering in a flat market is Fidelity Equity-Income (800-544-8888; $2,500 minimum investment; no load). Fund manager Stephen Peterson typically invests at least 65 percent of the fund's assets in stocks that have yields equal to or above the S&P 500's. The fund recently posted a 2.1 percent dividend yield vs. a 1.8 percent average dividend yield for the S&P 500. Moreover, the fund has returned 19.8 percent annually during the past five years vs. 17 percent for the typical large company value fund, and it's done so with approximately 40 percent less volatility than its average competitor.

Another solid fund is Scudder Growth & Income (800-225-2470; $2,500 minimum; no load), which invests in stocks with yields at least 20 percent higher than the S&P 500's. The fund's top two holdings recently were Xerox and Philips Electronics. During the past five years, the fund has gained 19.3 percent annually vs. 17.4 percent for its typical competitor.

T. Rowe Price Equity-Income (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum; no load) is another fund that could cushion your portfolio in a flat market. The fund recently posted a dividend yield approximately 1.5 percentage points higher than the S&P 500's. Furthermore, the fund has been approximately 50 percent less volatile than its typical competitor during the past five years.

Although still a relatively new fund, Montgomery Equity-Income (800-572-3863; $1,000; no load) warrants consideration. Fund manager John Brown only invests in stocks that have dividend yields 1.4 times the S&P 500's, and sells the stocks when the yields fall to the same level as the S&P 500's. Since its inception in September 1994, the fund has posted a cumulative return of 87.8 percent vs. 74.7 percent for the typical large-value company fund during the same time period.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a free-lance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
